The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on the interval $[-8,2].$ The graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is shown above, where the areas of the regions between the graph and the $x$-axis are $6,$ $5,$ and $4,$ respectively (from left to right). Find $f(0)$ if $f(-8)=-1.$

$f(0)=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
From the fundamental theorem of calculus, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-8}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(0)-f(-8) \\ {\int }_{-8}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =f(0)-(-1) \\ f(0) & =-1+{\int }_{-8}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, remember that the integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where we take the area as negative if the curve lies below the $x$-axis. So, using the labels on the graph, the integral is

$$
{\int }_{-8}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x=6+(-5)=1.
$$

Finally, using the value of the integral, we can find $f(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0) & =-1+{\int }_{-8}^{0}{f}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$
